objective: By the end of this lesson you can spot a nose-high or nose-low unusual attitude using only the instruments, recover in the right order to stable level flight, and explain how to prevent upsets and get back to VMC after flying into clouds by mistake.
why: Loss of control in flight is the leading cause of fatal general aviation accidents, and many start with a VFR pilot losing the horizon. A calm, correct recovery on instruments can save your life.

warmup: You are in a cloud, the airspeed is climbing fast and the altimeter is unwinding. Your body says you are level. What do you do with the throttle first, and why?

key_terms.def: An airplane attitude not normally needed for instrument flight, usually unintended.
Unintentionally exceeding normal flight: pitch more than 25 degrees up, more than 10 degrees down, bank more than 45 degrees, or wrong airspeed for the conditions.
Loss of control in flight: a big, unintended departure from the planned flightpath.
Your body senses disagree with what the airplane is really doing.
A descending turn that feels like a wings-level descent (no sense of turning); pulling back only tightens it.
Push forward enough to cut the G-load (about 1 G) before rolling level.
Inadvertent or unintended flight into instrument meteorological conditions (clouds, no horizon).
Single-pilot resource management: using every resource (autopilot, ATC, checklists, passengers) to stay ahead of the airplane.

chunks.title: How airplanes end up in unusual attitudes

body.p: An unusual attitude is an attitude not normally needed for instrument flight. Common causes: turbulence, disorientation, instrument failure, confusion, being busy with cockpit chores, a sloppy cross-check, misreading instruments, or weak aircraft control skills [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].
The FAA calls it an upset when you unintentionally go past these limits [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]:
The top causes of upsets that led to LOC-I accidents [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]:

bullets: Environmental: turbulence, wind shear, wake turbulence, icing [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
Mechanical (system and equipment failures): runaway trim, binding controls, autopilot problems, failed instruments that force partial-panel flying [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
Human: flying VFR into marginal VMC or IMC, diversion of attention, task saturation, spatial disorientation, surprise and startle [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Stall-related factors [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

body.p: Physiological factors are a big one. Spatial disorientation showed up in nearly 200 accidents from 2008 to 2013, and more than 70% of those were fatal [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. In a long, steady turn your inner ear stops sensing the turn. When you notice altitude loss and pull back, you just tighten the spiral: the graveyard spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

callout.text: A fast acceleration can feel like a nose-up pitch (somatogravic illusion), so a disoriented pilot may push into a dive [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Trust the instruments, not your body.

body.p: Prevention: get a good weather briefing, don't fly into marginal visibility (less than 3 miles) or into dusk and darkness unless you are trained and proficient on instruments, avoid sudden head movement, and be rested and healthy [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

check.a: Pitch more than 25 degrees nose up, more than 10 degrees nose down, bank more than 45 degrees, or airspeed wrong for the conditions [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].

body.p: Rule of thumb: any time an instrument moves at a rate or shows a reading that doesn't fit the maneuver you are flying, assume an unusual attitude. Speed up your cross-check to confirm whether it is the attitude, an instrument error or an instrument failure [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].
Don't worry about how you got there. The question is what the airplane is doing now and how to get back to straight and level fast [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
The same instruments show both; only the direction changes [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

callout.text: Don't depend on a spillable attitude indicator: it may have tumbled past its limits. Even a good non-spillable one can be off up to 5 degrees of pitch and bank and is hard to read in extreme attitudes. If in doubt, use the airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

body.p: Glass panels help. The PFD always keeps some sky and some ground showing so you can see the shortest way back [[23:216|IFH 7-55]]. Red chevrons appear at about 30 degrees nose up, or past 15 degrees nose down, and point back to the horizon. Past 60 degrees of bank, the roll index extends to show the shortest way to wings level [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

If the AHRS fails, all of that protection is gone, along with attitude and heading on the PFD [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. Then you use the standby instruments; the standby attitude indicator can tumble in extreme attitudes [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

check.q: Airspeed increasing, altimeter unwinding, turn coordinator showing a left turn. What attitude?

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the recovery

body.p: Use the recovery in your POH/AFM if it has one. If not, recover using the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. The generic FAA steps:
Nose-high (airspeed decreasing or below what you want) [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]:

bullets: 1. Add power, in proportion to how fast you are slowing down.
2. Forward elevator pressure to lower the nose and prevent a stall.
3. Level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder: level the miniature airplane and center the ball.
Do these almost at the same time, but in this order. Level pitch shows when the airspeed and altimeter needles stop and reverse.

body.p: Nose-low (airspeed increasing or above what you want) [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]:

bullets: 1. Reduce power to stop excess speed and altitude loss.
2. Level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, using the turn coordinator.
3. Raise the nose to level with smooth back pressure.
In training, do it by the numbers in this order. Your instinct will be to pull back first. Don't: in a bank that tightens the turn.
Keep a fast cross-check for overcontrolling; the first control inputs may be large.
When the altimeter and airspeed needles slow, stop and reverse, you are passing through level flight.
As airspeed, altimeter and turn coordinator settle, bring the attitude indicator back into the scan.
Center the ball; slips and skids feed disorientation.
If you started from an assigned altitude, climb or descend back to it once stable.

body.p: The AFH gives a general upset recovery template too [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]:

For a spiral dive (nose-low, steep bank, speed building): 1. power to idle, 2. a little forward elevator to unload to about +1 G, 3. roll wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder, 4. gently raise the nose, 5. at Vy, climb power and climb back to a safe altitude [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

head: What the examiner wants (ACS)
Standard
rows: Use proper instrument cross-check and interpretation to identify an unusual attitude (including both nose-high and nose-low) in flight (ACS PA.VIII.E.S1)
Apply the appropriate flight control, power input, and aircraft configuration in the correct sequence, to return to a stabilized level flight attitude (ACS PA.VIII.E.S1)
Use single-pilot resource management (SRM) or crew resource management (CRM), as appropriate (ACS PA.VIII.E.S2)
This Task lists no numeric altitude or heading tolerances; airspeed limits (Vne, Va) and configuration come from your POH

check.a: Reduce power, level the wings, then raise the nose smoothly [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

chunks.title: Stay inside the envelope: smooth, proportional inputs

body.p: An untrained pilot reacts to a surprise attitude by instinct, with abrupt muscle force. That is hazardous in turbulence, at high speed and at low altitude [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[24:109|AFH 5-4]].

bullets: Match your control and power inputs to how much and how fast the airplane is rolling, pitching and changing speed, so you don't overstress it (unless the ground is about to be hit) [[24:109|AFH 5-4]].
Nose-high: the threat is a stall. Lower the nose; the critical angle of attack, not airspeed, is what stalls the wing [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].
Nose-low: the threat is overspeed and overstress. A spiral dive can be at or past Vne, so raise the nose slowly and gently [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
Never pull hard while rolling level. A rolling pullout exceeds the airplane's design limit more easily and can cause structural damage or failure [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

callout.text: Nose-low: Power off, Push (unload), Roll, then Pull gently. Never roll and pull hard at the same time [[24:131|AFH 5-26]] [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

body.p: Control input errors that cause unusual attitudes in the first place: poor trim (a distraction while holding pressure leads straight into one) [[23:189|IFH 7-28]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. During the recovery itself, watch for overcontrolling, since the first inputs may be large [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

check.q: Why unload before rolling level from a spiral dive?
check.a: Pushing to about +1 G lowers angle of attack and G-load and prevents a rolling pullout that can exceed the design limit [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

bullets: An autopilot or wing leveler reduces workload, gives you time to monitor, and lowers the chance of an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

After an AHRS failure, all autopilot modes except roll and altitude hold are lost [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. With AHRS and air data failed and no attitude shown, one manufacturer recommends turning on the autopilot, which then works only as a wing leveler [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].
But a malfunctioning or misused autopilot can cause an upset. Disconnecting it lets you fly the airplane directly and may remove the cause [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
Step 1 of the upset recovery template is to disconnect the wing leveler or autopilot; failing to do it is a common error [[24:111|AFH 5-6]] [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].
Keep hand-flying skills sharp, including partial panel, so a failure doesn't become an upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

callout.text: Know your own system before you need it: which modes survive which failures, and where the disconnect is. That comes from the POH/AFM supplement.

check.q: You are in an upset with the autopilot engaged. First action from the AFH template?
check.a: Disconnect the wing leveler or autopilot [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

chunks.title: Into the clouds by mistake: getting back to VMC

body.p: Untrained pilots, or pilots whose instrument skills have faded, lose control in about 10 minutes once they must fly by instruments only [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. If you can't hold attitude by the natural horizon, you are in IMC, whatever the weather report says. Treat it as a real emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Three first steps: accept that it is serious, keep control of the airplane, and get help to get safely on the ground [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

bullets: Trust the instruments. Don't fly partly on instruments while searching outside for the horizon [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].
Don't panic. Your one job right now is to keep the wings level [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].
Trim for hands-off level flight at cruise speed; use fingertip pressure; change pitch by no more than one bar width [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].
Use the autopilot or wing leveler if you have one [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].
Turn back toward VMC with no more than 10 degrees of bank. For a big heading change, turn a few degrees, level, and repeat [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].
Climb: nose up no more than one bar width and add power. Descend: reduce power in small steps and never exceed 500 fpm [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].
Avoid climbing or descending turns [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

body.p: Get ATC on the radio. Radar facilities can give vectors to a VFR pilot in difficulty [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. Keep the controller told about the weather you are in and ahead, and [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]:

bullets: If a route to VFR weather and a safe landing exists, take it instead of a vector or approach into IFR weather.
If you can't stay VFR, tell the controller you are not instrument rated and declare a distress condition.
If you are instrument rated, current and equipped, request an IFR clearance.

body.p: If you are already talking to ATC, keep your assigned code. If you can't reach ATC right away, squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]; it normally sets off an alarm at radar control positions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]. Ask for help early: you are in at least an urgency condition the moment you are doubtful about weather or anything that could affect safety [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

callout.text: ATC may sound urgent. Don't let it rush you into a maneuver that loses control. It's fine to ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

body.p: When you break out, give yourself time to get oriented before trying to land, even if that means flying straight and level or circling for a while, especially at night [[24:371|AFH 18-22]].

check.q: Max bank for turns when a VFR pilot is in IMC?

bullets: Distraction: setting avionics, hunting for charts, or a system problem can pull your eyes off the instruments long enough to enter an upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].
Task saturation and stress: an upset can happen whenever the job exceeds your skill, like a tired pilot in night IMC with a vacuum failure [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Loss of situational awareness: many upsets happen while busy with a task that takes attention away from the instruments [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Surprise and startle: train with realistic scenarios so a real upset doesn't freeze you [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

body.p: Collision hazards: under the hood you can't see out. Simulated instrument flight requires a safety pilot with at least a private pilot certificate for the category and class, and the safety pilot must have adequate vision forward and to each side (or a competent observer on board must make up for it) [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109]]. Instructors and safety pilots tend to look inside too much during hood work and forget see-and-avoid [[16:15|AC 90-48E, 17.2]]. For stall practice the IFH advises a safe altitude, an area free of conflicting traffic and radar traffic advisories; use the same care for unusual attitude practice [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Most midair collisions happen in good VFR weather, in daylight [[24:31|AFH 1-10]].
SRM in an upset [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]:

bullets: State the situation clearly and briefly.
With two pilots, give control to the one with the best situational awareness.
Use standard calls and work as a team to manage stress.
Single pilot: keep an organized cockpit and trim the airplane so a moment's distraction doesn't become an emergency [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

callout.text: Prevention happens in minutes and hours (planning and risk management). Proportional counter-response happens in seconds [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]. Recovery skills are for the upset you could not avoid [[24:109|AFH 5-4]].

check.q: Who must be in the other seat for hood work?
check.a: A safety pilot with at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Read airspeed trend first: decreasing = nose-high, increasing = nose-low
Power off, wings level, then raise the nose
Not disconnecting the autopilot; not unloading; rolling the wrong way [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
Follow the template: disconnect, push, roll to nearest horizon
Bad airspeed management in the recovery [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]
Add power nose-high, reduce power nose-low
Adding power or pulling while rolling in a spiral dive [[24:132|AFH 5-27]]
Idle, unload, roll, then gently pull
Slow cross-check and fixation (stop and stare) [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Cross-check several instruments; one alone can lie
Poor trim and a messy cockpit [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Trim always; organize charts and devices before flight
Forgetting to return to the assigned altitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]
Once stable, go back to the original altitude

body.p: Practice: with a CFI and the hood, close your eyes while the instructor sets up an attitude, then open them and recover on the CFI's call. Do both nose-high and nose-low, full panel and partial panel. These skills are perishable, so repeat them [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

check.q: Name two common upset recovery errors from the AFH.
check.a: Any two: wrong assessment of the upset, not disconnecting the autopilot, not unloading, rolling the wrong way, poor airspeed management [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

scenario.title: Haze, a tablet and a sinking turn
scenario.setup: You are a student pilot on a solo cross-country at dusk. Visibility is dropping in haze over dark, rolling farmland with few lights. You look down at your tablet to find the next frequency. When you look up there is no clear horizon. The engine sounds louder, the airspeed is near the top of the green arc, the altimeter is unwinding, and you feel level.

questions.q: What is happening, and why do you feel level?
questions.a: Likely a nose-low descending turn (spiral). In a steady turn the inner ear stops sensing it, so it feels wings-level; pulling back would tighten the spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

questions.q: What is your recovery, in order?
questions.a: Reduce power, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder using the turn coordinator and attitude indicator, then raise the nose smoothly to level [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. Unload slightly before rolling if the G-load is high [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

questions.q: What must you avoid with the airspeed near the top of the green and still building?
questions.a: A hard pull while rolling. A spiral dive can reach or pass Vne, so roll level first, then raise the nose slowly and gently to avoid overstress [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

questions.q: You are level again but still in haze. Now what?
questions.a: Keep the wings level and trimmed, turn toward better weather with no more than 10 degrees of bank, call ATC, tell them you are a student pilot not instrument rated and declare an emergency if you can't stay VFR [[24:368|AFH 18-19]] [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

questions.q: What went wrong before the upset, and how do you prevent it next time?
questions.a: Continued flight into marginal visibility at dusk, plus heads-down distraction. Set frequencies before the busy phase, keep the cockpit organized and trimmed, and turn back before visibility gets marginal [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

skills.do: Under the hood, the examiner puts the airplane in a nose-high or nose-low attitude and gives it back to you. Identify it from the instruments and recover with power, pitch and bank in the right order to stable level flight.
skills.practice: With a CFI, close your eyes during setup, then recover on command, both nose-high and nose-low, full and partial panel [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

skills.do: Use SRM: say what you see, use available automation correctly, keep the cockpit organized, and keep watching for traffic.
skills.practice: Call out the attitude and each step aloud during practice; brief your safety pilot before hood work [[24:111|AFH 5-6]] [[16:15|AC 90-48E, 17.2]].

quiz.q: Airspeed decreasing, altimeter climbing, turn coordinator showing a right turn. Using the IFH unusual attitude procedure (no POH procedure), your first action?
options: Pull back to stop the climb
Roll left to level the wings
quiz.why: Nose-high: add power in proportion to the slowdown, then forward elevator, then level the wings [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

quiz.q: In a nose-low unusual attitude, what is the correct order?
options: Raise the nose, level the wings, reduce power
Reduce power, level the wings, raise the nose
Level the wings, add power, raise the nose
Raise the nose, reduce power, level the wings
quiz.why: Reduce power, level the wings with coordinated controls, then smoothly raise the nose [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

quiz.q: The FAA defines an upset as pitch more than ___ nose up, more than ___ nose down, or bank more than ___.
quiz.why: Pitch more than 25 degrees up, more than 10 degrees down, bank more than 45 degrees [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].

quiz.q: How do you know you are passing through level pitch during recovery?
options: The airspeed and altimeter needles stop and reverse
quiz.why: When the altimeter and airspeed needles stop and reverse direction, the airplane is passing through level flight [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

quiz.q: Why should you NOT pull hard while rolling out of a spiral dive?
options: A rolling pullout can exceed the design limit and cause structural failure
quiz.why: The design limit is exceeded more easily in a rolling pullout [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

quiz.q: About how long does an untrained VFR pilot keep control after losing visual references?
A non-instrument-rated pilot can't stay in VFR conditions. Per the AIM, what should the pilot tell ATC?
options: Say they are not instrument rated and declare a distress condition
quiz.why: Advise the controller of no instrument rating and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

quiz.q: On a glass PFD, the AHRS fails. What happens to unusual attitude protection?
options: It switches to the standby instruments
quiz.why: With an AHRS failure, all unusual attitude protection is lost, along with attitude and heading on the PFD [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

takeaways: Any odd instrument rate = assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check.
Nose-high: power up, nose down, wings level. Nose-low: power off, wings level, nose up gently.
Never pull hard while rolling; unload first in a spiral dive.
If the attitude indicator might be bad, recover on airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator.
In IMC by mistake: wings level, trim, turns of 10 degrees or less, call ATC early.
Prevention beats recovery: weather, trim, an organized cockpit, and staying out of marginal visibility.
cfi_notes: Teach the airspeed trend as the first clue: it instantly tells nose-high from nose-low, even with a failed attitude indicator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
Watch for the instinctive pull in nose-low entries; insist on power first [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

Include partial panel entries; an attitude indicator that has tumbled or failed is a real cause and the recovery then relies on airspeed, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].
Eyes-closed entries remove surprise; add realistic distractions in scenarios to train against startle [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Brief collision avoidance and positive exchange of controls before every hood session; the CFI is the lookout [[16:15|AC 90-48E, 17.2]].
Point out that the IFH nose-high sequence (power, pitch, bank) and the AFH upset template (disconnect, unload, roll, power) differ; the POH comes first [[23:188|IFH 7-27]] [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].
gaps: The prompt said AFH chapter 4; in AFH FAA-H-8083-3C, upset prevention and recovery is Chapter 5 (Ch 4 is energy management). Chapter 5 was used.
The ACS Task has no numeric tolerances; airspeed limits (Vne, Va), power settings and the airplane's own recovery procedure come from the POH/AFM.
Sources give no single named procedure like a standard 180-degree turn for IIMC; the lesson uses AFH 18 guidance (shallow turns of 10 degrees or less toward VMC) and AIM 6-2-1.
Autopilot mode behavior after failures varies by installation (IFH describes one system); check the POH/AFM supplement.

The sound of the airplane speeding up

Roll the wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder

activities.title: True or false: envelope and automation

cards.s: In a nose-high attitude, the main danger is a stall.
cards.why: Yes. That is why you lower the nose with forward elevator pressure, to prevent a stall [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

cards.s: To get out of a spiral dive fast, roll level and pull back hard at the same time.
cards.why: No. A rolling pullout exceeds the airplane's design limit more easily and can cause structural damage or failure. Unload, roll level, then raise the nose gently [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

cards.s: Your control and power inputs should match how much and how fast the airplane is rolling, pitching and changing speed.
cards.why: Yes. Proportional inputs avoid overstressing the airplane, unless ground contact is about to happen [[24:109|AFH 5-4]].

cards.s: On a glass panel, the autopilot keeps all of its modes after an AHRS failure.
cards.why: No. In the IFH example, all autopilot modes except roll and altitude hold are lost [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

cards.s: A malfunctioning or misused autopilot can cause an upset.
cards.why: Yes. Disconnecting it lets you fly the airplane directly and may remove the cause [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

cards.s: Step 1 of the AFH upset recovery template is to add full power.
cards.why: No. Step 1 is to disconnect the wing leveler or autopilot. Power is adjusted later, in step 4, by watching airspeed [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

activities.title: Stuck in a cloud: what now?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then the right action.

pairs.r: No more than 10 degrees of bank, a few degrees at a time
Nose up one bar width at most, then add power
Reduce power in small steps, never more than 500 fpm

pairs.l: Can't stay VFR, no instrument rating
pairs.r: Tell ATC and declare a distress condition
Ask the controller to slow down

final_quiz.q: Which of these is a mechanical factor that can cause an upset, according to the AFH?
final_quiz.why: Runaway trim is a mechanical failure that can directly cause a departure from normal flight. Wake turbulence and icing are environmental factors, and task saturation is a human factor [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: During training, your CFI sets up a 35 degree bank with the nose 20 degrees up while your eyes are closed. How does the AFH classify this?
options: An upset, because the bank is past 30 degrees
An unusual attitude, but not an upset
final_quiz.why: An upset is unintended and goes past 25 degrees nose up, 10 degrees nose down or 45 degrees of bank. This setup is on purpose and inside those limits, so it is an unusual attitude only [[24:106|AFH 5-1]] [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

final_quiz.q: You look up from your tablet and see this panel. Your POH has no unusual attitude procedure. What do you do first?
options: Pull back firmly to stop the altitude loss
Add power to protect against a stall
Raise the nose, then level the wings
final_quiz.why: Airspeed increasing and altitude dropping in a left turn means nose-low. First reduce power, then level the wings, then raise the nose smoothly. Pulling back first would tighten the turn [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

final_quiz.q: You fly an older airplane with a spillable attitude indicator. In a steep nose-up attitude you think it may have tumbled. With no POH procedure, which instruments do you use to recover?
options: The attitude indicator alone, once it settles
Airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator
final_quiz.why: Don't depend on a spillable attitude indicator, since its limits may have been exceeded. Start the recovery using the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and turn coordinator [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

final_quiz.q: In the glass panel system described in the IFH, when do the red chevrons appear in a nose-low attitude?
final_quiz.why: For nose-low attitudes the chevrons show when pitch goes past 15 degrees nose down. If the AHRS fails, all unusual attitude protection is lost [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

final_quiz.q: You are recovering from a spiral dive and the airspeed is near Vne. The wings are now level. How should you raise the nose?
options: Pull firmly so the altitude loss stops fast
Add full power, then pull up to a climb
Slowly and gently, climbing only once the speed drops to a safe level
Quickly to a steep climb to burn off the extra speed
final_quiz.why: The airplane may be at or past Vne, so inputs must be slow and gentle to prevent structural failure. Raise the nose to a climb only after speed decreases to safe levels [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these is a common error in spiral dive recovery listed in the AFH?
options: Unloading to about +1 G before rolling
Rolling the wings level before raising the nose
final_quiz.why: Mistakenly adding power is a listed error. The other three are correct steps of the recovery [[24:132|AFH 5-27]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: Your CFI has you close your eyes while setting up each unusual attitude. According to the AFH, what does this take out of the training that a real upset would have?
options: The need to use the instruments
final_quiz.why: With eyes closed during setup, any element of surprise disappears. Realistic distractions in scenario training help prepare you for real startle [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: You are VFR, not instrument rated, and just flew into a cloud heading north. Clear air is behind you. How should you turn back to the south?
options: A 30 degree bank turn, held all the way around
A climbing turn to get on top of the clouds
Small turns of no more than 10 degrees of bank, leveling the wings between them
A steep 45 degree bank turn to get out fast
final_quiz.why: Use the smallest practical bank, never more than 10 degrees. For a big heading change, turn a few degrees, level, and repeat. Avoid climbing or descending turns [[24:368|AFH 18-19]] [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

final_quiz.q: Still in the cloud, you need to descend to get below it. Your airplane is trimmed for level cruise. How should you descend?
options: Lower the nose two bar widths and keep cruise power
Reduce power about 100 rpm at a time, keeping the descent at 500 fpm or less
Pull the power to idle and spiral down
Make a descending turn toward where the clear air was
final_quiz.why: Reduce power in steps of 100 rpm or 1 inch of manifold pressure, never exceed 500 fpm, and keep pitch within one bar width below level [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].

final_quiz.q: You are lost in haze and not talking to any ATC facility. You can't raise anyone right away. What should your transponder show?
final_quiz.why: If you can't reach ATC right away, squawk 7700, the emergency code. It normally sets off an alarm at radar control positions [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]] [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].

final_quiz.q: You want to practice unusual attitude recoveries under the hood in a Cessna 172. Who may sit in the other control seat as your safety pilot?
options: A private pilot with an airplane single-engine land rating
A student pilot with 40 hours in the 172
A private pilot with only a glider rating
Any passenger who agrees to watch for traffic
final_quiz.why: The safety pilot needs at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the airplane, and adequate vision forward and to each side [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109]].

final_quiz.q: Which habit best keeps a short cockpit distraction from turning into an unusual attitude?
options: Holding a firm grip on the yoke
Always flying with the autopilot off
Keeping the airplane trimmed for level flight
final_quiz.why: Failing to keep the airplane trimmed can turn a momentary distraction into an emergency. The IFH also says using the autopilot lowers the chance of an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].
